title: The urls table
idea: The `urls` table stores each short code, target and owner. `user_id` is a foreign key: its value must match a row in `users`.
points: The database checks every rule on every insert, even from code that skips Zod.
`unique` refuses a repeated `short_code` and adds an index for fast lookups.
`varchar(10)` caps the code length. `nanoid(7)` fits with room to spare.
Drizzle maps `shortCode` in JavaScript to `short_code` in SQL.

parts.label: JS property
parts.note: The name you use in queries: `urls.userId`.

parts.label: Column
parts.note: An integer column called `user_id` in Postgres, the same type as `users.id`.

parts.label: Required
parts.note: Every URL needs an owner. An insert without `user_id` is refused.

parts.label: Foreign key
parts.note: The value must match an existing `users.id`. An unknown user is refused.

parts.label: On delete
parts.note: Deleting a user also deletes their URLs, so none is left without an owner.

code.title: src/db/schema.js
code.caption: The `urls` table is the new part. Postgres refuses two bad inserts, then a delete cascades.

walk.text: A repeated `short_code` is refused. Ten characters is the longest code the column accepts.
The target is required text. Lecture 13 already limits it to `http` and `https`.
The foreign key: required, must match a `users.id`, and removed together with its user.
Setup: the same tables as SQL. In the project, a migration creates them.
The same code for another user is refused. `23505` is Postgres's unique-violation code.
An owner that does not exist is refused. `23503` is the foreign-key code.
Delete Ada. `cascade` removes her two URLs, so one link is left.

pitfalls: Do not check for an existing code in JavaScript first; two requests can both pass.
Editing `schema.js` does not change the database. Apply the change with a migration.
Use `cascade` only when a URL is meaningless without its user.

quiz.q: Ada is user 1 and owns the only row in `urls`. What does this print?
options: It throws a foreign key error
quiz.why: `onDelete: 'cascade'` deletes the user's URLs with the user. Without it, Postgres would refuse the delete while URLs still point at that user.

takeaway: Put uniqueness and ownership rules in the schema, so the database enforces them.

starters: What is the difference between a foreign key and just storing an id?
When should I not use onDelete cascade?
Why is short_code a varchar(10) and not plain text?
